phrases.english_text: I was the only one that was White, and the rest of them were Cherokee. It wasn’t until I was six years old that I spoke Cherokee. I was always fighting with Tom’s boys, because we couldn’t understand each other. When they would bring them, we didn’t understand what we were saying. My uncle and my aunt—my aunt watched out for me growing up. My mom worked in Decatur and got on the bus in Bentonville. They left at three in the morning. Artie Green drove the bus. And in the evening, they got back around five or six. And one morning… one evening Mom said, when she came back… I was six years old, my uncle and my aunt didn’t speak English, they only spoke Cherokee. I was listening to that. And Mom said, “One day when I got off the bus, all of a sudden you spoke Cherokee.” I was speaking Cherokee ever since.
So, you must’ve learned Cherokee pretty easy?

phrases.english_text: Let’s see. A long time ago, me and Lawrence Eagle went to Cherokee, North Carolina and had a revival for a week. When we got to Cherokee, North Carolina, if you weren’t listening well, it was hard to understand. They still speak that old dialect, “like for instance,” I was telling him. “If we say car as we know it—big eyes. Headlights, that’s what it, that’s what it amounts to. We’re talking about its headlights, dig(a)tulen(i).” Over there it’s adladidla, ᎠᏜᏗᏜ. And, here [Oklahoma Cherokee say] “What time is it?” Hila atliili, ᎯᎳ ᎠᏟᎢᎵ? Eastern Band Cherokee for the same question is ‘how many times did it tick?’ / ᎯᎳ ᏳᏩᏂᎸ / hila iyuwanilv?

phrases.english_text: I was telling some people this: we went towards the Rising of the Sun (North Carolina) one time. It was over 20 years ago. When we got there, we were looking around. There weren’t hardly any Cherokee speakers there in town. And when we were leaving there, there was a man that passed by that looked native. He came and we started talking. And then I noticed this old man really speaks Cherokee. Then I started speaking Cherokee and immediately he started replying in Cherokee. I could understand him fully, he was putting it a little different, but that was the first time I heard somebody speaking in the East. I could understand him fully. And still to this day, that old man is still alive. And that’s what I was telling people—the younger ones do it a little different than the way he spoke. That next generation is hard to understand. I was having difficulties, sometimes I can’t understand what they’re saying.

phrases.english_text: I was telling some people this: we went towards the Rising of the Sun (North Carolina) one time. It was over 20 years ago. When we got there, we were looking around. There weren’t hardly any Cherokee speakers there in town. And when we were leaving there, there was a man that passed by that looked native. He came and we started talking. And then I noticed this old man really speaks Cherokee. Then I started speaking Cherokee and immediately he started replying in Cherokee. I could understand him fully, he was putting it a little different, but that was the first time I heard somebody speaking in the East. I could understand him fully. And still to this day, that old man is still alive. And that’s what I was telling people—the younger ones do it a little different than the way he spoke. That next generation is hard to understand. I was having difficulties, sometimes I can’t understand what they’re saying.

We were doing that every weekend, visiting each other. They would be playing dominoes or playing cards. Sitting there until midnight. The late, Ulud(i) had a ’50 model flatbed truck. It was a rough ride. His wife’s name was Sal(i). The boy they raised—Tsudu they called him. He would be looking out of the truck, driving by, this [gestures] would be happening, like it was a plane [his hand]. They would park it—if they rode in the truck. We were visiting each other. They cooked back then—nobody cooks nowadays—as I was growing up, my late aunt, Sil(i) was her name. She was Alits(i)’s wife. Then I grew up and I was working. They worked in Decatur, Alits(i) and his daughter, Didi—they called her Lucinda. When they would leave at three o’clock, then Sil(i) and I would get up. And in the living room, there hanging on the ceiling was where she made quilts. “Kam,” she’d say to me. “Get up!” she’d say. She’d wake me up at three am. She was teaching me how to sew quilts. When I got married, I had seven quilts that I had made myself. My mom was teaching me to cook. “If you don’t ever get married, at least you’ll know how to sew and cook, so you won’t be starving. Or you might get married, and she might die before you. Or if you get divorced, you will not have to bother anyone. You would know how to take care of yourself,” that’s what they taught me.

phrases.english_text: I guess about four years ago, I like to visit the elders. That’s how I grew up, we visited the elders all the time. I like to listen to what they knew. When I got back here, from prison, I went to visit them. My grandma and grandpa was sitting there and there were children about four, five, or six years old, they were running around. They were speaking all in English. They didn’t understand Cherokee, or speak it. My grandparents were sitting over here and they weren’t speaking English. They were speaking all in Cherokee. The kids couldn’t understand them. And then the kids were talking in English so the grandparents couldn’t understand them. I felt bad about that. We’ve already lost that much. There’s nobody teaching them Cherokee. A person that speaks Cherokee is going to talk English to the kids.

They were speaking all in English. They didn’t understand Cherokee, or speak it. My grandparents were sitting over here and they weren’t speaking English. They were speaking all in Cherokee. The kids couldn’t understand them. And then the kids were talking in English so the grandparents couldn’t understand them. I felt bad about that. We’ve already lost that much. There’s nobody teaching them Cherokee. A person that speaks Cherokee is going to talk English to the kids.

Yeah, that’s true. When I was growing up, one time, I was about 16 years old. The lumber yard hired me on. There was a long trailer loaded with lumber. On top, back then, it used to look like this [gestures]. And on the roof, it was like plastic. There were four of us men. I was only a boy. We were there all day. We were, then we were, stacking them up. The others were White and there was one Cherokee. They made a bet. “That boy that is following us around, working with us. He’s going to leave soon,” they said. “How much do you want to bet?” There was one there, among them, that said, “No, I think he’s going to be here all day.” Even the one that owned the lumber yard was thinking the same. He thought I wasn’t going to be there all day. But I worked all day. And they were really surprised. I was only around 15 years old and I was there that long. I wasn’t that big back then, I was skinny. [laughs] The owner said, “Boy! I didn’t think you was gonna last that long, Chief,” he said. “I had to, cause Mom chased me over here!” I told him. [laughter] “I’m going to pay you as much as I did these grown up guys,” he told me. That’s how much he gave me, and it was $40, and that was probably a lot for back then.

phrases.english_text: Witsigal(i) was saying, we were laughing at him, “They called us to go into the Army,” he said. “We didn’t have a choice then. phrases.english_text: Have you all noticed that when a Cherokee speaks—I don’t know if y’all’ve noticed, if not, next time pay attention—when a full-blood Cherokee speaks English, they say “He,” when they’re talking about a woman. If I don’t think about what I’m going to say, "If I don’t’ think about what I’m going to say, first,” I tell people. “I’ll say it backwards. If I talk too fast,” I tell them.

phrases.english_text: Have you all noticed that when a Cherokee speaks—I don’t know if y’all’ve noticed, if not, next time pay attention—when a full-blood Cherokee speaks English, they say “He,” when they’re talking about a woman. And when they talk about a man, they say “She.” They say it backwards. And it’s all the Cherokee that does that. That happens to me, too. If I don’t think about what I’m going to say, "If I don’t’ think about what I’m going to say, first,” I tell people. “I’ll say it backwards. If I talk too fast,” I tell them.
If you talked about Mitch, you’re going to say “She.” [laughs]
“She interviewed me,” I’m gonna say.

phrases.english_text: Those Wolfes that live in Kenwood …But [they’re] the ones that came later. There was an old woman, her Cherokee name was Susan(i). She had one boy that she raised, they called him Hotshot. He was always out drinking. Even when he was a young boy, he was already getting locked up in jail. One time, the police chased him and they were shooting at him. When he got to his mom’s all the police pulled up. “Where do you take my boy?” she said. “Oh, we gotta take him to jail,” they said. “How come?” she asked. “’Cause he’s drunk,” they said. They took him. There was a store in Kenwood, owned by a White man. But he understood Cherokee, since there were a lot of Cherokee there he had to have learned it. She went into the store and said, “I’m Ms. Wolfe.” He asked her, “What can I do for you today, Ms. Wolfe?” “I want a phone,” she said. “Right there it is!” he said. – “I want to use the phone.” “Go ahead!” he said. She picked up the phone and said, “Hello, jail?”

phrases.english_text: Also, one time we were talking about him—his name was Gas(i). He was taking a motor out of a truck. He had already taken the motor out, and it was sitting by him. His wife said, “Gas(i) we’re running out of flour.” “Really?” [he asked] Then he thought about it. Then he got in the truck and went down the hill all the way to the road. Somebody pulled up and asked him, “What’s wrong, Gas(i)?” He said, “I can’t get the truck started!” Because there wasn’t a motor in it! And he was telling the truth! He said, “It’s not making a sound when I turn the key.” He was telling the truth, there was no motor in it. “Where you headed?” they asked. “Just over to the store,” he said. “Alright, I can probably push your truck there!” they said. And they pushed him all the way to the store. He went and bought what he needed. And outside there was a bench where the old men sit. Gas(i) got in the truck and he was telling the men that he couldn’t get it to start. “I can’t get it to start,” he said. “Well, we’ll try to push you!” they said. They pushed him going backward. When they got to the road they pushed him again, but it still didn’t do anything. Then after a while, somebody pulled up, “What’s wrong, Gas(i)?” “We can’t get it to start!” he said. “Alright, I’ll push you!” he told Gas(i). They pushed him all the way home. There wasn’t a motor inside it.

They would bring it for me to cook. It was that Cornish Hen and ramen noodle with the seasoning [packet] in it. That’s what I used for my broth. Then I cut up chicken and boiled it. Then when I thought it was about ready, when it was really done; then I would put tortillas in hot water, when they got firm I would make them round. Then I would get a can of coke and I would roll the [tortilla] dough with that. When I got it thin enough then I would cut them up and put them in [the broth]. That’s what I did for dumplings. I don’t like my dumplings gooey. I like them to have a little texture and I want them to be firm. That’s the way I fixed them. And boy did they eat it. They always made me cook. When it was Christmas all the prisoners bought food. Sometimes I made 30 pizzas by myself. I made them this [gestures] big. I just put them on cardboard.

phrases.english_text: --or smell me, when they got home. I was laying down. Outside on the porch, there was a fence about this [gestures] tall. It had a latch with a spring. I heard that and I thought they were home. So, I covered my head. When the door opened, I heard the screen door, it opened and closed. Something came in the house, and somebody knocked. [Thump] It knocked as it went along. The hair on the back of my neck was standing straight up. I was still covered up. When it got to the kitchen, the plates, boy, they started breaking. Like it was throwing them around, and also like it picked up a chair and threw it. The way it sounded. I was about ready to get up and run then I saw [car] lights. They were home. As soon as they came in the house, I jumped up and ran in there. “Boy, something is in the house!” I told Sil(i): “He tore up the kitchen. I don’t know what it was, but the plates are all broken on the floor.” She turned the light on in the kitchen. There wasn’t anything scattered on the floor. It was funny to her. There was a reason why they left the leftover food on the table. If there wasn’t anything on the table, boy it would throw a fit. Sil(i) started cooking right away. She cooked salt meat and bread and put it on the table. And things got quiet.
